title: Assyrian Blasphemy
english: Rabsaces, the messenger of the king of Assyria, addressed Hezekiah with a message from his master, saying that the great king of Assyria wished to know on whom Hezekiah relied for support, since he had rebelled against him.

Rabsaces pointed out that Egypt, on whom Hezekiah seemed to be relying, was a broken reed that would pierce the hand of anyone who leaned on it, as he said, 'Behold, you trust in the staff of Egypt, which is a broken reed, and whoever leans on it will pierce his hand' (Isaiah 36:6).

The king of Egypt, Pharaoh, was not a reliable ally, and those who trusted in him would be disappointed, for Rabsaces called him a broken reed, saying that all who trust in him will be wronged, rather than benefited.

When a city was besieged and its walls were manned by brave warriors, the need for ambassadors was clear, and the chosen representatives of the king would go out to negotiate with Rabsaces, who was known for his harsh and boastful speech.

Rabsaces blasphemed against the glory of God, saying 'Is it by counsel or words of lips that a battle array is formed?' (Isaiah 36:4), implying that the Jews' trust in their wisdom and knowledge of the law would not save them from the Assyrian army.

The Jews thought themselves wise and blessed because they had the law of Moses, and indeed they said, 'We are blessed, Israel, because we know what is pleasing to the Lord' (Isaiah 36:10), but Rabsaces argued that this would be of no use to them in the face of the enemy.

Rabsaces believed that Hezekiah did not trust in God, but rather in the Egyptians who possess the land, and that this hope was fragile and easily broken, much like a reed that will surely break if someone leans on it, and will wrong the one who trusts in it.

The commander's words were laced with blasphemy, as he lifted up his horn and spoke injustice against God, challenging the Judeans to make a deal with his lord, the king of Assyria, if they truly trusted in the Lord their God.

He said, 'if you say: We trust in the Lord our God, now make a deal with my lord the king of Assyria, and I will give you two thousand horses, if you can provide riders for them' (Isaiah 36:8), and 'how can you resist the face of just one of the Assyrian governors?'

Furthermore, Rabsaces said, 'if you have trusted in Him, make a deal with my lord, that is, arm yourselves and stand for battle, and I will add, and give you two thousand horses, and this will be enough' (Isaiah 36:9).
Rabsaces also called Hezekiah by name only, without adding 'king', which was a title most becoming for a ruler, and he referred to the king of Assyria as not simply a king, but a great king.

The Jews, having the law through Moses, thought themselves wiser than other nations, but Rabsaces brought down their boast of war and battle, saying that it will be completely useless for them to have knowledge of laws, and to be wise in counsel, and to have only words.

title: Divine Sovereignty and the Humbling of Pride
english: How is it that you, grasping at nothing but vanity, did you not hear these things long ago—the very things I have done? If you truly desire to occupy yourselves with the words of my prophets, I have already declared, even before they came to pass, that these events would occur. For from the earliest days I have established and ordained all things, setting them in their proper order.

Now I have revealed the appointed time, when the foretold judgments come to their fulfillment, so that nations shall be laid waste even in their fortified cities—not the weak, but the strong and seemingly secure. I stretched out my hands, and they withered and dried up.

He who once held them together, sustaining them in existence and establishing the hand that avenges, I have removed; and now the grass withers equally, the herbs fade like straw, and the dry stalks become fuel for the fire.

Thus also he says elsewhere to him: Since the impious, passing through what God has ordained, has grown proud in his own heart, he again heard God saying, 'Shall the axe boast itself against the one who hews with it? Or shall the saw exalt itself above the one who draws it?' For just as these tools do not move themselves to work by chance, but wait for the hand that shakes them, so you have become an instrument of my divine wrath.
Yet you did not act by your own strength; you were like an axe and a saw, moved only by the will of the one who uses you. And now I know your rest and your going out.

Your wrath, which you once burned with, and your bitterness have risen up against me. He boasts, having become a servant of the divine judgments, perhaps imagining in his heart that he alone has been magnified by conquering these nations and lands, as he has burned them and taken them captive. But I know your rest, and your going out, and your coming in.

He calls rest what I name death, and going out and coming in, the way to every undertaking. For nothing at all escapes the mind that knows all things. He adds, saying that your wrath, which you once burned with, and your bitterness have risen up against me, that you shall not go unpunished for having been slandered.

For I will not at all look upon your wicked thoughts, the evil and the bitter, but as one provoked to grief by your dispositions, I will impose upon them their proper justice. And I will put a bridle in your nose, and a bit in your lips, and I will turn you back by the way by which you came.

Since the Assyrian, having the folly of beasts most conspicuously, mocked God, and as it were having rushed into wildness like a beast, he sent forth the sounds of the glory of God, in this way moreover very fittingly as concerning beasts he says, I will put a bridle in your nose, and a bit in your lips, not only by the leadings of the plagues.
